Lecture 24

Fourier operational rules and distributional transforms

Lecture objectives

We prove the operational rules of the Fourier transform for integrable functions and check them on a Gaussian wave packet. We prove that exponential decay of a function makes its transform analytic in a strip. We define the transform of a tempered distribution by duality and compute the transforms of deltas, constants, sinusoids and the step, and we write the step as a regularized integral over wave numbers.

Lecture 23 defined the Fourier transform of an integrable function, computed the transforms of a rectangular pulse, a Gaussian and decaying exponentials, and proved two inversion theorems. In this lecture we derive rules that produce new transforms from known ones. They describe the effect of a shift, a modulation, a change of scale, a derivative and a multiplication by x.xx. We then show that a function with exponential decay has a transform that is analytic in a strip of the complex kkk-plane. Finally, we extend the transform to the tempered distributions of Lecture 22. The extension assigns transforms to the delta, to constants and sinusoids, and to the step, none of which is integrable. The lecture reads in three stages: the ordinary rules and the strip (Sections 24.1–24.2), duality (Section 24.3), and the distributional pairs with the card (Sections 24.4–24.5).

24.2 Analyticity in a strip

Lecture 18 showed that the transform of a Gaussian extends to an entire function of k,kk, because of the fast decay of the Gaussian. Exponential decay of fff already gives analyticity of f^\widehat ff​ in a strip. For a>0a>0a>0 let Ua={k∈C:∣Im⁡k∣<a}U_a=\{k\in\C:\abs{\Im k}<a\}Ua​={k∈C:∣Imk∣<a} be the open strip of width 2a2a2a about the real axis.

The proof below applies Lecture 18’s lemma on analytic parameter integrals to the entire functions k↦e−ikxf(x).k\mapsto\ee^{-\iu kx}f(x)k↦e−ikxf(x).

Theorem 24.7 (Strip of analyticity). Let fff be piecewise continuous on every bounded interval, let a>0,a>0a>0, and let ∫Rea∣x∣∣f(x)∣ ⁣dx<∞.\int_{\R}\ee^{a\abs x}\abs{f(x)}\dd x<\infty .∫R​ea∣x∣∣f(x)∣dx<∞.(24.7) Then for every k∈Uak\in U_ak∈Ua​ the integral f^(k)=12π∫Re−ikxf(x) ⁣dx\widehat f(k)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{\R}\ee^{-\iu kx}f(x)\dd xf​(k)=2π​1​∫R​e−ikxf(x)dx converges absolutely. The continuity property licenses regularization: approximate a tempered distribution by integrable functions, transform them as functions, and take the limit.

The transform is defined on S(R)\Schwartz(\R)S(R) rather than on the smaller class D(R)\testspace(\R)D(R) for the following reason. For ψ∈D(R)\psi\in\testspace(\R)ψ∈D(R) condition (24.7) holds for every a>0,a>0a>0, so ψ^\widehat\psiψ​ extends to an entire function by Theorem 24.7. So ψ^∉D(R)\widehat\psi\notin\testspace(\R)ψ​∈/D(R) for every nonzero ψ∈D(R),\psi\in\testspace(\R)ψ∈D(R), and a distribution that acts only on D(R)\testspace(\R)D(R) cannot be paired with ψ^.\widehat\psiψ​. The function ex\ee^xex of Lecture 22 defines such a distribution, which is not tempered, and it has no Fourier transform in the sense of Definition 24.11.

The operational rules extend to tempered distributions. We use Lecture 22’s definitions of translation, scaling and multiplication, with tests ψ∈S(R),\psi\in\Schwartz(\R)ψ∈S(R), for multiplication by xxx and by eiαx\ee^{\iu\alpha x}eiαx only: multiplication by an arbitrary smooth function does not preserve S(R)\Schwartz(\R)S(R) (ex2e−x2=1).\ee^{x^2}\ee^{-x^2}=1ex2e−x2=1). The functions ψ(⋅+x0),\psi(\cdot+x_0)ψ(⋅+x0​), ψ(⋅/c),\psi(\cdot/c)ψ(⋅/c), xψx\psixψ and eiαxψ\ee^{\iu\alpha x}\psieiαxψ lie again in S(R),\Schwartz(\R)S(R), with seminorms bounded by finite combinations of seminorms of ψ,\psiψ, so these operations produce tempered distributions from tempered distributions.

24.4 Distributional transforms

We now compute the transforms of the basic tempered distributions of Lecture 22. None of them is an integrable function, so none has a transform in the sense of Lecture 23.

Summary

The shift, modulation, scaling and conjugation rules hold for every integrable function. The derivative rule needs a continuous function with an integrable derivative; a jump adds a term that only the distributional derivative records. Exponential decay makes the transform analytic in a strip. The multiplication formula moves the transform onto tests in S(R);\Schwartz(\R)S(R); this defines the transform of every tempered distribution, such as deltas, constants, sinusoids and the step.

  • Rules: the first table of Section 24.5, each with its hypotheses; F ⁣[f′]=ikf^\FT{f'}=\iu k\widehat fF[f′]=ikf​ needs a continuous f.ff.

  • Strip: if ∫ea∣x∣∣f∣ ⁣dx<∞\int\ee^{a\abs x}\abs{f}\dd x<\infty∫ea∣x∣∣f∣dx<∞ with a>0,a>0a>0, then f^\widehat ff​ is analytic on ∣Im⁡k∣<a;\abs{\Im k}<a∣Imk∣<a; for e−a∣x∣\ee^{-a\abs x}e−a∣x∣ the strip ∣Im⁡k∣<a\abs{\Im k}<a∣Imk∣<a cannot be widened.

  • Tempered transforms: ⟨T^,ψ⟩=⟨T,ψ^⟩\distpair{\widehat T}{\psi}=\distpair{T}{\widehat\psi}⟨T,ψ⟩=⟨T,ψ​⟩ for ψ∈S(R);\psi\in\Schwartz(\R)ψ∈S(R); the pairs of the second table; ex\ee^xex is not tempered and has no transform.

  • Step: in the sense of tempered distributions, 1/(k−iε)→pv⁡(1/k)+iπδ;1/(k-\iu\varepsilon)\to\pv(1/k)+\iu\pi\dirac1/(k−iε)→pv(1/k)+iπδ; for x≠0,x\ne0x=0, (2πi)−1∫eikx ⁣dk/(k−iε)=e−εxΘ(x);(2\pi\iu)^{-1}\int\ee^{\iu kx}\dd k/(k-\iu\varepsilon)=\ee^{-\varepsilon x}\Heaviside(x)(2πi)−1∫eikxdk/(k−iε)=e−εxΘ(x); at x=0x=0x=0 the principal value is 12.\tfrac1221​.

The transform of a product is not the product of the transforms; Lecture 25 shows that the transform of a convolution is.

Self-check

4 questions. Answer without looking back at the notes; a first miss gives a hint and a second try. Enter numbers with a decimal point.

1. Let fff be integrable and g(x)=f(2(x−a))g(x)=f(2(x-a))g(x)=f(2(x−a)) for real aaa. Which formula for g^(k)\widehat g(k)g​(k) holds for every such function and shift under the course’s negative forward sign?

Hint. Solve the substitution u=2(x−a)u=2(x-a)u=2(x−a) for xxx before changing the phase and the measure.

The substitution gives x=a+u/2x=a+u/2x=a+u/2 and  ⁣dx= ⁣du/2\dd x=\dd u/2dx=du/2. The phase splits into e−ikae−i(k/2)u\ee^{-\iu ka}\ee^{-\iu (k/2)u}e−ikae−i(k/2)u, so the result is 12e−ikaf^(k/2)\tfrac12\ee^{-\iu ka}\widehat f(k/2)21​e−ikaf​(k/2). The other expressions omit the Jacobian, reverse the sign of the shift phase, or scale the actual shift aaa by another factor of two.

2. Let f(x)=3e−xΘ(x)f(x)=3\ee^{-x}\Heaviside(x)f(x)=3e−xΘ(x). If you differentiate on each open side of zero and apply the ordinary Fourier derivative rule without checking continuity, you miss a delta at zero. Find the coefficient of that delta in the distributional derivative. Round to two decimal places.

Enter a valid number using a decimal point.

Hint. When integrating by parts on the two half-lines, compare the one-sided limits at zero.

The ordinary derivative on the two sides is −3e−xΘ(x)-3\ee^{-x}\Heaviside(x)−3e−xΘ(x). Its missing boundary contribution is the jump from 000 to 333, so the distributional derivative also contains 3δ(x)3\dirac(x)3δ(x). The ordinary rule assumes continuity across the join. The distributional rule includes the transform of the extra term, 3/2π3/\sqrt{2\pi}3/2π​.

3. Let f(x)=e−2xf(x)=\ee^{-2x}f(x)=e−2x for x>0x>0x>0 and f(x)=e3xf(x)=\ee^{3x}f(x)=e3x for x<0x<0x<0. Write the Fourier variable as k=ξ+iηk=\xi+\iu\etak=ξ+iη with real ξ\xiξ and η\etaη. On which maximal open strip does the defining Fourier integral converge absolutely and give an analytic function?

Hint. Multiply both tails by the modulus of e−ikx\ee^{-\iu kx}e−ikx, then test each end separately.

The phase modulus is eηx\ee^{\eta x}eηx. The positive tail decays if η−2<0\eta-2<0η−2<0, and the negative tail decays if η+3>0\eta+3>0η+3>0. These strict inequalities give −3<η<2-3<\eta<2−3<η<2 and uniform exponential bounds locally inside that strip. Swapping the endpoints reverses the forward sign. The narrower symmetric strip is only a sufficient substrip, and the wider one admits a divergent positive tail.

4. In the sense of tempered distributions, what is the Fourier transform of Θ(x)\Heaviside(x)Θ(x) with the course’s unitary negative-sign forward convention?

Hint. Use the derivative to determine the odd part and reflection to determine the even part.

The derivative is δ(x)\dirac(x)δ(x), so multiplication of the transform by ik\iu kik gives 1/2π1/\sqrt{2\pi}1/2π​. Since kpv⁡(1/k)=1k\pv(1/k)=1kpv(1/k)=1, the principal-value term has the displayed sign. A delta at zero is invisible to this multiplication. Reflection gives Θ(x)+Θ(−x)=1\Heaviside(x)+\Heaviside(-x)=1Θ(x)+Θ(−x)=1, so the even part of the step is 1/21/21/2. Its transform is π/2 δ(k)\sqrt{\pi/2}\,\dirac(k)π/2​δ(k). Omitting or doubling the delta gives the wrong even part, and changing the principal-value sign gives the wrong derivative.
